extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical geometry, mechanics, and hydrostatics (readers of Archimedes)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted theorems, postulates, assumptions and lemmas from Archimedes' The Sand-Reckoner, Quadrature of the Parabola, and On Floating Bodies (Book I). These are canonical geometric and physical propositions and numerical conventions used in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption — perimeter of the earth
rubrics_metrics.description: (Perimeter of earth) + 3,000,000 stadia. [Assumption 1]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a numerical hypothesis in subsequent bounds (e.g., to estimate earth's diameter and further derive bounds on the 'universe').

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption — relative diameters (sun, earth, moon)
rubrics_metrics.description: By hypothesis, d_z > 30 d_m, and d_e > d_mn. [Assumptions 2–3 referenced].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These comparative size assumptions (sun, earth, moon) are employed to bound ratios of diameters and infer inequalities used in estimates of cosmic sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption 5 — poppy-seed and grain counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose a quantity of sand taken not greater than a poppy-seed contains not more than 10,000 grains; suppose diameter of poppy-seed ≥ 1/4 finger-breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This empirical bound is used to scale up counts of grains for spheres of increasing diameter to estimate total number of grains fitting the 'universe'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric scheme — orders and periods of numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a naming/ordering scheme: traditional names up to 10,000; these form first-order numbers up to 10,000^2 = 100,000,000; define successive orders and periods using 100,000,000 as base unit, iterating to create hierarchies (P, P', P*, etc.) up to extremely large indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This systematic notation permits expression and manipulation of astronomically large numbers; explanatory table and index-based representation are provided to show scale (e.g., last number of first period requires 1 followed by 800,000,000 ciphers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem on continued proportion (geometric progression property)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a geometric progression with first term 1 and second 10 (1,10,10^2,...), the product of two terms Am and An is itself a term in the series, located as many terms distant from A1 as An is from Am; algebraically Am·An = A_{m+n−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses proportionality of equally distant terms in a continued proportion; used to manipulate indices and justify multiplicative relations among terms in the octad/period scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application — scaling spheres to grains of sand
rubrics_metrics.description: Using poppy-seed assumptions and volumetric scaling (spheres scale as cube of diameter), compute number of grains in spheres of diameters scaled by factors of 100 repeatedly; use terms of the geometric series to place these numbers into the order/period scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides stepwise table mapping sphere diameters (finger-breadths → stadia → millions of stadia → ... → 'universe') to corresponding term indices in the number scheme to conclude bounds on grains in universe-sized spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion — bound on number of grains in universe-sized sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Using earlier bounds, the number of grains of sand in a sphere of the size of our 'universe' is less than 1,000 units of the seventh order of numbers (i.e., less than 10^{?} as per the scheme), and the sphere of fixed stars contains less than 10,000,000 units of the eighth order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final quantitative claims derived from Assumptions and the number-naming scheme; intended to show that a finite (though enormous) number suffices to count 'all the sand'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate — upper bound of 'universe' diameter in stadia
rubrics_metrics.description: (diameter of ‘universe’) < 10,000 (diameter of earth), and hence (diameter of ‘universe’) < 10,000,000,000 stadia (using assumed perimeter and conversions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by geometric inequalities relating perimeters of inscribed polygons and assumed ratios between celestial diameters; used in grain-count estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometrical proposition (implicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: If α, β are circular measures of two angles (each < right angle) with α > β, then tan α / tan β ≈ sin α / sin β (text references equivalent trig formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as equivalent to a proposition assumed earlier; used in angular/distance estimations (contextual remark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrature Prop. 1 — chord parallel to tangent property
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a point P on a parabola a line is drawn which is either the axis or parallel to it (PV), and QQ' is a chord parallel to the tangent at P meeting PV in V, then QV = VQ'. Conversely, if QV = VQ' then QQ' is parallel to the tangent at P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes chord symmetry w.r.t. diameter/axis; used to relate chord lengths and tangent orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrature Prop. 2 — equality of segments to tangent intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: If QQ' is a chord parallel to the tangent at P, and a line through P (axis or parallel) meets QQ' in V and the tangent at Q in T, then PV = PT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates distances along diameters/axes to tangent intersections; used in later constructions and doubling arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrature Prop. 3 — proportionality of segments
rubrics_metrics.description: If from P a diameter PV is drawn and from two other points Q, Q' lines are drawn parallel to the tangent at P meeting PV in V, V', then PV:PV' = QV^2:QV'^2 (proportion relating lengths squared in the ordinate system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a continued-proportion relationship among ordinates and diameters; used to derive coordinate-like relations of the parabola.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrature Prop. 4 — ratio relation QV:VO = OF:FR
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a parabolic segment with base Qq and vertex P; with diameter through another point R meeting Qq in O and QP (produced) in F, then QV:VO = OF:FR (relating chord/diameter partitions to segments on the diameter through R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent to change of axes (coordinate transform) arguments; proof uses parallels and continued proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrature Prop. 5 — ratio relation QO:Og = ER:RO
rubrics_metrics.description: If Qq is base of a parabolic segment, P vertex; diameter through some point R meets Qq in O and tangent at Q in E, then QO:Og = ER:RO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Prop. 4 and doubling arguments; used to establish proportions among diameters and tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 6 & 7 — centre of gravity for triangle using lever
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a horizontal lever AOB supported at midpoint O, a triangle BCD suspended at points yields equilibrium when a weight P at A equals 1/3 of triangle ABCD area (i.e., P = 1/3 ABCD); the midpoint of certain constructed segment is the triangle's centre of gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive lever-based proof identifies center of gravity location and shows how an area representing 1/3 of triangle balances the triangle; separate cases handle right or obtuse angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 8 & 9 — inequalities for balancing a triangle vs area
rubrics_metrics.description: With a triangle suspended appropriately from two points on a lever, an area P that balances the triangle satisfies P < ABCD but P > Q (for a specified area Q defined via lever ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives bounds on balancing areas relative to triangle and a comparison area Q through lever geometry and centre-of-gravity placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 10 & 11 — trapezium balancing gives P < Q
rubrics_metrics.description: For a trapezium CDEF placed so parallel sides are vertical and suspended from two points, if AO:OH = (trapezium):Q then the area P that keeps lever equilibrium satisfies P < Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs center-of-gravity via parallel lines and midpoints; uses divisions of lever arm to compare resulting balancing area with Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 12 & 13 — sandwich bounds for balancing area
rubrics_metrics.description: If AO:OH = (trapezium):Q and AO:OL = (trapezium):R for different suspension points, then the balancing area P satisfies R < P < Q (P > R but < Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows monotonic dependence of balancing area on suspension point location; uses centre-of-gravity construction to derive inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 14 & 15 — polygonal/trapezoidal approximations give bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide base Qq into equal parts, construct trapezia and triangles inscribed between the parabola and diameters; then the area of the parabolic segment is bounded: A_EqQ < 3(sum of certain trapezia + last triangle) and A_EqQ > 3(sum of other trapezia + last triangle), establishing upper and lower Riemann-like sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are early integral-approximation style inequalities used to squeeze the segment area via inscribed trapezia and triangles; they are crucial for the later limit/contradiction arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 16 — segment area equals 4 × area of A E q Q
rubrics_metrics.description: If Qq is base of a parabolic segment and E is point where line through q parallel to axis meets tangent at Q, then area of segment = 4 × area(A E q Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by contradiction using the earlier approximations: assume area greater or less than 4× and derive impossibilities by subdividing and comparing trapezia/triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 17 — area of parabolic segment = 4/3 of inscribed triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Every segment bounded by a parabola and a straight line is four-thirds of the triangle with the same base and equal height (area(segment) = 4/3 × area(PQq)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines Prop. 16 with geometric relations showing A E f q Q = 4 × A P Q q and concludes the classic 4/3 result; includes definition of base, height, and vertex of a segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 18 — vertex identification via midpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: If Qq is base of a parabolic segment and V is midpoint of Qq, and diameter through V meets curve in P, then P is the vertex of the segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Prop.1 (parallel chord–tangent property) to show the perpendicular from P to the base is maximal, hence P is the vertex by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 19 — diameter relationships (PV and RM)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Qq is a chord bisected in V by diameter PV, and RM is a diameter bisecting QV in M, then PV = 4 RM (a relation among diameters/ordinates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from the parabolic proportionalities giving PV:PW = QV^2:RW^2 and algebraic manipulation; used to relate scales of successive doublings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 20 — triangle greater than half the segment
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parabolic segment with base Qq and vertex P, the inscribed triangle PQq is greater than half the area of the segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangle PQq is half of the parallelogram formed by chord, tangent, and diameters, which exceeds the segment; corollary: one can inscribe a polygon so that leftover segments are less than any assigned area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 21 — area splitting: A_PQq = 8 × A_PRQ
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is vertex of the segment cut off by PQ, then area APQq = 8 × area APRQ (and more generally inscribed triangles in successive segments relate by factor 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses diameter bisections and previous PV/RM relations to compute area ratios for successively smaller segments; supports geometric series construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 22 — series of areas each 4× next sum less than segment
rubrics_metrics.description: If A, B, C, D,... are areas with each equal to four times the next and the largest A equals triangle PQq, then A + B + C + ... < (area of the parabolic segment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: inscribed triangles in the iterative segmentation produce an inscribed polygon whose area (sum) is less than the full segment; used to bound sums from below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 23 — geometric series identity (algebraic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given areas A, B, C,... with A greatest and each four times the next, then A + B + C + ... + Y + Z = (4/3) A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic manipulation of a geometric series with ratio 1/4 yields sum 4/3 A; this identity is used to compare constructed polygonal sums to the target segment area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 24 — every parabolic segment equals 4/3 triangle (final)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining earlier propositions and series arguments, every segment bounded by a parabola and a chord Qq equals K = (4/3) × area(PQq); i.e., area(segment) = 4/3 area of the inscribed triangle with equal base and height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final synthesis: contradiction arguments rule out area being greater or less than K; uses Propositions 14–23 to establish equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 1 (On Floating Bodies) — fluid continuity and thrust
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a fluid of such character that its parts lie evenly and continuously, that parts less thrust are driven by those more thrust, and that each part is thrust by the fluid above it in a perpendicular direction if the fluid is depressed or compressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational physical assumption (axiom) about fluid behavior underpinning all subsequent hydrostatic propositions; used to reason about equilibrium and pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating Bodies Prop. 1 — spherical surface criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a surface is cut by every plane through a certain point and every section is a circle whose centre is that point, then the surface is a sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric uniqueness of spheres: equality of radii to all points on sections implies spherical surface—used to deduce shapes of fluid surfaces under gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating Bodies Prop. 2 — fluid surface at rest is spherical
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of any fluid at rest is the surface of a sphere whose centre is the same as that of the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Postulate 1 and contradictions: if a section were not a circle centered at earth's centre, unequal compressions would set fluid in motion. Concludes that gravitational equipotential surfaces are concentric spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating Bodies Prop. 3 — immersion of solids equal in weight to fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: Solids which, size for size, are of equal weight with a fluid will, when let down into the fluid, be immersed so that they neither project above the surface nor sink lower (they float exactly level with surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs pyramids and compares pressures to show that such solids cannot project above nor sink; an early equilibrium/neutral-buoyancy statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating Bodies Prop. 4 — solids lighter than fluid do not fully submerge
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid lighter than a fluid will, when immersed, not be completely submerged: part of it will project above the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contradiction argument analogous to Prop. 3: complete submersion would create unequal pressures and motion; thus lighter solids float partially above surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating Bodies Prop. 5 — Archimedes' principle (equilibrium version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any solid lighter than a fluid, placed in the fluid, will be so far immersed that the weight of the solid equals the weight of the fluid displaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proof using pyramids and pressure equality at corresponding sections; establishes buoyant equilibrium condition used throughout hydrostatics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating Bodies Prop. 6 — buoyant force when forcibly immersed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid lighter than a fluid is forcibly immersed in it, the solid will be driven upwards by a force equal to the difference between its weight and the weight of the fluid displaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration by hypothetically adding weight to the solid to equate it to fluid weight and then inferring upward driving force when that additional weight is removed; formalizes net buoyant force = displaced fluid weight − body weight.
